rationale: A wins because it builds four different editor permissions: engagement data, efficacy fight, monetization mechanics, and category expansion, then tells you what proof each desk will demand. Its strongest line, "A profitable public company is giving away chess and charging for the AI," is an actual business story, not confetti. B has usable bones, but "A profitable, public Duolingo posts a record 40% jump in daily active users — is the growth story still intact?" is too close to a company milestone wearing a reporter hat, and it keeps sneaking in unsupported framing like "The video feature is in beta now."
gaps_in_A: "Duolingo says people are talking to its cartoon owl" is factually sloppy: the update says users talk with Lily, not the owl. Cute headline, wrong character.
"live, unscripted spoken conversation" adds "unscripted" without support. Do not smuggle product behavior into the angle because it sounds stronger.
"its most-criticized design" overstates the supplied fact. We know some educators criticized gamification as shallow learning; we do not know it is Duolingo's most criticized design.
"the company thinks its asset is the habit loop" is a smart inference, but it needs an executive quote before it becomes pitchable.
gaps_in_B: "The video feature is in beta now" is wrong or unsupported; the update says beta engagement averaged 9 minutes and the feature is launching for paid Max subscribers.
"AI tutors that actually engage" turns a usage metric into a broad AI-tutor claim. Nine minutes proves engagement, not tutoring quality.
"Duolingo is responding by adding more engagement-driven AI features" and "Duolingo is doubling down" invent motive, and "double down" is on the cliché blacklist for a reason.
"a gamified chess course" is not in the update. Duolingo may gamify courses, but this fact set only says a chess course launches free.
